source.title: A Neural Scaling Law from the Dimension of the Data Manifold

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figure labels are flattened or OCR-like.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss against parameter count in teacher/student networks and image classifiers, using power-law fits. It tests model-size scaling in settings different from the original language-model study.
record.gate_note: The GPT scaling exponent and claims about LSTM/Transformer similarity are cited from other work, not new loss-scaling results here. The paper measures GPT activation intrinsic dimensions, recorded as a result with no matching claim version. The study does not test token- or compute-scaling or a compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: The study fits loss against parameter count in new settings: synthetic teacher/student networks with effectively infinite data, and small CNNs on CIFAR10, MNIST, Fashion MNIST and SVHN. These results bear on whether the power-law form holds beyond language-model pretraining (V5). It also reports where power-law scaling ends (V7). The GPT part only measures activation intrinsic dimension and cites the loss exponent from Kaplan et al., so it does not test V1. The method resembles the original (log-log fits of L vs N), but the setting is new, so T3 fits better than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue α ≈ 4/d for ReLU networks with MSE or cross-entropy loss, with α ≥ 4/d as a bound in non-generic cases such as product manifolds. They report this confirmed in teacher/student and CIFAR10 experiments. For GPT, measured d > 90 satisfies d ≥ 4/α ≈ 53 but is far from equality, and the discrepancy is left unexplained.
record.recipe_differences: Uses power-law fits of loss against parameter count, but mainly on synthetic teacher/student models and image classifiers; it does not reproduce the original language-model sweep or test token and compute scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: The power-law fitting window is selected from the tested points; scaling ends through overfitting on finite image datasets and optimization or numerical-precision limits in teacher/student experiments. GPT activation ID varies with layer, estimator, and whether tokens come from distinct sequences or one contiguous passage.

fits_no_version.finding: CIFAR10 error rate scales with N with an exponent close to the loss exponent (test 4/α 16.23 vs 17.83).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Image-classification error rate follows a power law in model size with an exponent similar to the loss exponent.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-2 small activation ID is over 90 for the last token across layers, but about 7 within one contiguous passage. This is consistent with α ≥ 4/d using the cited exponent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-scaling exponents relate inversely to the intrinsic dimension of the learned data manifold (α ≈ 4/d generically, a bound otherwise).

record.problems: The image experiments have a train/test gap, and finite image datasets can overfit. Scaling breakdown in teacher/student experiments is attributed to optimization or numerical-precision issues without a complete explanation. Intrinsic-dimension estimates may have systematic errors, especially at large dimensions; the GPT result relies on a scaling exponent cited from other work. Some Nmax estimates use an arbitrary threshold and extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately quantified rows omitted. Cited GPT scaling results and cited cross-architecture comparisons were not recorded as rows because they are results from other work.

untested.parts: No new language-model pretraining loss sweep; the GPT exponent is cited from KMH+20.
No extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
Student depth varies (2–4 layers), but the effect of shape on loss at fixed N is not quantified.
Video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. Data and compute scaling are not tested. Only model-size scaling over about one to one-and-a-half orders of magnitude is covered.
Disagreement between published laws, parameter counting, schedule and fitting-method comparisons are not tested.

missing.what: Empirical Nmax, the end of the power-law region for 2-layer students, versus ID: log Nmax = 0.2d+5.95 (CE) and 0.17d+6.35 (MSE). The breakdown is attributed to optimization or numerical precision.
Deeper students (3–4 layers) extend power-law behaviour to larger N and lower loss than 2-layer students, while 2-layer students are best for k>5 in the fitted range.

record.verdict_notes: Co-authored by Kaplan but not an original source. Model-size ranges are small (about 10^3–10^4 parameters), so the study does not show scaling over several orders of magnitude. The GPT part provides no new loss-scaling data.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not itself test held-out pretraining loss scaling in language models; its GPT loss exponent is cited. Its own scaling experiments are teacher/student and image-classification settings.
No small-run fits are tested as predictors of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and tokens is tested.
The paper varies student depth in some experiments but does not test whether depth and width change loss only slightly at fixed parameter count.
The study tests synthetic teacher/student experiments and image-classification models, not video, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
It reports image-classification error-rate scaling, but not downstream task performance after language-model pretraining or performance predicted from pretraining loss.

The study reports scaling-region endpoints and describes breakdowns, but does not test disagreements between published exponents or compare alternative parameter-counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices systematically.

rows.subject: fully connected student networks (random-teacher experiment)
rows.operation_detail: Fit cross-entropy loss against parameter count for students trained to imitate random teachers.

conditions.value: online random inputs; effectively infinite dataset

rows.measure: Power-law loss scaling exponent and measured intrinsic dimension
rows.value: The reported aggregate result is 4/α ≈ d; the measured ID increases by about 10% from the smallest to largest student sizes.
rows.note: Aggregate result stated by the paper across the teacher/student experiments; the paper reports separate feature-count curves in figure 5.
rows.check: The measure is the 4/α–ID relation. What bears on V5 is that L(N) follows a power law for every k = 2–19 (figure 5). Observed holds for the power-law form, over roughly 10^3–10^4 parameters.

rows.subject: teacher/student experiments
rows.operation_detail: Estimate the largest network size in the power-law region as a function of intrinsic dimension using a fixed loss threshold.

conditions.value: For some low-feature teachers, estimated by extrapolating the power-law fit

rows.measure: Relationship between log Nmax and intrinsic dimension
rows.value: log(Nmax) = 0.45d + 0.69 for cross-entropy; log(Nmax) = 0.84d + 0.54 for MSE.
rows.note: The threshold is described as arbitrary; some Nmax estimates extrapolate beyond the tested networks.
rows.check: Nmax here is defined by an arbitrary loss threshold of 6e-3, with extrapolation for low-k teachers. It is not an observed bend of the curve. The empirical end of the power-law region is in figure 12, which no row records.

rows.subject: ‘small’ 117M parameter GPT-2 model
rows.operation_detail: Measure intrinsic dimension of activations from the last token in 10,000 distinct text sequences, across attention, fully connected and residual outputs.

conditions.value: test data from the same distribution as training data
nearest-neighbor and MLE; results vary by layer and estimator

rows.value: The authors conclude d > 90 for the relevant last-token activations; the cited scaling exponent gives 4/α ≈ 53. ID is roughly constant across layers except the first, and a single contiguous 1024-token passage gives ID ≈ 7.
rows.uncertainty: The paper notes substantial possible systematic error; MLE histograms include reported spreads in appendix figures.
rows.locator: Section 3.4; figures 10 and 11; appendix figures 17 and 22
rows.note: This is an activation-dimension measurement, not a new language-model loss-scaling sweep. The scaling exponent is cited from [KMH+20].

relationships.condition: Synthetic teacher/student (CE, MSE, generalized losses, product manifolds) and CIFAR10 CNNs
relationships.reason: Power-law L(N) fits hold across all teacher feature counts and losses (R1–R6). CIFAR10 test and train loss also follow power laws in the tested range (R7, R8).
relationships.display_finding: Loss followed power laws for every tested teacher feature count and loss function, and CIFAR10 training and test losses followed power laws within the tested range.

relationships.reason: The authors say the power-law trends on these datasets are less clear than on CIFAR10, with short fitted ranges (R9–R11).
relationships.display_finding: Power-law trends were less clear than on CIFAR10 and were fitted over short ranges.

relationships.reason: Based on the text (figure 12, appendix A.1), not on rows. Power-law scaling ends at an Nmax even without data limits, attributed to optimization or precision failure. Deeper students extend the region, and the fit window is chosen by a circle-fit rule.
relationships.display_finding: Power-law scaling ends at a maximum model size despite effectively infinite data, attributed to optimization or precision failure, while deeper students extend the scaling region and a circle-fit rule determines the fitting window.
